Tracked large debris.provides: known orbit, predictable conjunctions, days of warning

Untracked millimetre debris.provides: no warning of any kind, high flux, damage rather than destruction

Spent rocket body.requires: an expended upper stage left in orbit
Spent rocket body.provides: large uncontrolled mass, tracked, cannot manoeuvre, breakup risk

Low Earth orbit.provides: high relative velocities, dense debris population, atmospheric decay over years

Sun-synchronous polar.requires: a specific inclination and altitude band
Sun-synchronous polar.provides: crowded operational band, head-on conjunction geometry

Geostationary belt.provides: low relative velocities, sparse population, no atmospheric decay ever

Highly elliptical transfer.provides: crossing traffic at many altitudes, brief exposure per pass

Ground radar catalogue.requires: objects large enough to return a radar echo
Ground radar catalogue.provides: routine tracking of large objects in low orbits, poor at high altitude

Optical telescope survey.provides: tracking of high-altitude objects, useless in daylight or cloud

Onboard collision sensor.requires: a sensor fitted and a detectable approach
Onboard collision sensor.provides: seconds of notice at best, effectively none for closing velocities in orbit

Operator conjunction message.provides: days of notice for cooperative satellites only

Propulsive avoidance manoeuvre.requires: working propulsion, fuel, and hours of notice
Propulsive avoidance manoeuvre.provides: reliable miss distance, fuel cost, service interruption

Attitude change to reduce cross-section.provides: reduced probability, no change of trajectory

Shielding already fitted.requires: a design decision made before launch
Shielding already fitted.provides: protection against small impacts only, no action needed at the time

Days.requires: a tracked object and routine conjunction screening
Days.provides: time for planning and propulsive action

Hours.requires: a late catalogue update or a refined solution
Hours.provides: time for a rushed manoeuvre only

None.requires: an untracked object or a sensor-only detection

_v1_notes.OBJECT CLASS|ORBIT REGIME: untracked millimetre debris in the geostationary belt is N - the population there is sparse and relative velocities are low enough that the hazard class does not apply as posed.
_v1_notes.OBJECT CLASS|WARNING SOURCE: untracked debris gives no warning from radar, optics or operators; only an onboard sensor could register it, and then only at impact. Onboard sensors are N for tracked debris, satellites and rocket bodies, which are seen far earlier by other means. Operator conjunction messages are Y only for active satellites, since debris and spent stages have no operator.
_v1_notes.OBJECT CLASS|MITIGATION: untracked debris admits no manoeuvre and no attitude change - there is no warning to act on - leaving acceptance and pre-fitted shielding. Shielding is N against large tracked objects, satellites and rocket bodies, which would destroy the spacecraft regardless.
_v1_notes.OBJECT CLASS|LEAD TIME: untracked debris gives no lead time at all, so days and hours are N; everything tracked gives days or hours but not none.
_v1_notes.ORBIT REGIME|WARNING SOURCE: optical survey is N for low Earth orbit and sun-synchronous, where radar is the practical sensor; radar is N for the geostationary belt, where optics take over.
_v1_notes.WARNING SOURCE|MITIGATION: an onboard sensor is N for propulsive manoeuvre and N for attitude change - by the time it registers anything there is no time to act. Radar, optics and operator messages are all N for shielding, which is not a response to a warning.
_v1_notes.WARNING SOURCE|LEAD TIME: radar, optics and operator messages all give days or hours, never none. An onboard sensor gives none, never days or hours.
_v1_notes.MITIGATION|LEAD TIME: propulsive manoeuvre and attitude change are both N with no lead time.
